title: Immune memory: recognise, respond, remember
subtitle: Build a defence model and explain a faster second response
objective: Explain how barriers and the specific immune response protect the body, including memory after immunisation.

sow.exactOutcome: Explain the body's defences & immune response.
sow.alignment: Directly develops Pearson 5.12–5.14; antibiotics are a short 5.16 contrast. Core mechanism is Foundation-accessible. This is a conceptual model, not medical advice.

priorLearning: A line graph shows change using stated axes.
success: Connect a barrier with how it reduces entry.
Distinguish an antigen, an antibody and a memory lymphocyte.
Use a graph to explain the faster secondary response to the same antigen.

vocabulary.meaning: A defence that reduces entry of pathogens.
A molecular feature recognised by the immune system that can trigger a specific response.
A protein that binds to a specific antigen and helps defend against it.
A type of white blood cell involved in specific immune responses.
A long-lived lymphocyte that supports a faster response to a previously encountered antigen.
Stimulating protection against a disease, commonly by vaccination.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one selected response route; pen, ruler and calculator.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint. Optional word processor or spreadsheet.
preparation: Print the shared evidence page, one chosen response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the teacher answers before teaching. All numerical sample data in this lesson are constructed for learning.
safety: Paper and screen tasks; no biological sampling, cultures, medicine handling or personal health disclosures.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is included. Point, annotate, dictate or discuss quietly instead of writing or using a device.

misconceptions.claim: Antibodies are tiny white blood cells.
misconceptions.correction: Antibodies are proteins; lymphocytes are cells involved in making them.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to put protein or cell beside each word.

misconceptions.correction: Binding is specific to antigen features; the diagram is a simplified fit model.
misconceptions.check: Offer antigen X and Y in the matching task.

misconceptions.correction: Immune memory can give a faster response and reduce disease risk/severity; protection is not an absolute guarantee.
misconceptions.check: Ask why the graph is not a prediction for every individual.

misconceptions.correction: Antibiotics act against bacteria; vaccination stimulates an immune response and memory.
misconceptions.check: Match each intervention to its mechanism.

access.supported: Same core scientific goal, with word bank, short prompts, read-aloud or pointing/dictation. Do not assign a route from diagnosis.
access.standard: Use the supplied evidence to explain and justify an independent scientific decision.
access.stretch: Optional challenge after secure core: evaluate a limitation and transfer the science. Higher-tier-only material, where present, is labelled explicitly.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer solo or partner work, a pass and quiet response. Allow a brief reset and re-entry at the next numbered task; no compulsory disclosure, performance or speed competition.

slides.title: How can the second response be faster?
body: Mission: build a defence explanation from cells, proteins and evidence.
Use the model; no personal health stories needed.
slides.notes: Invite prediction. Explain that “memory” is a property of immune cells, not a person remembering to fight an infection.

slides.title: Three distinctions
body: R1. What is a pathogen?
R2. What does a physical barrier do?
R3. Is a cell the same thing as a protein?
slides.notes: R1 disease-causing agent. R2 reduces entry. R3 no: a cell contains many molecules; antibody proteins are made by cells. Teach protein as a type of molecule without requiring amino-acid detail.

slides.title: Before a specific response
body: Match a structure with its protective action.
I explain how it works, not just where it is.
slides.notes: Model: “Mucus traps particles/pathogens. Cilia move mucus towards the throat, helping remove them from the airways.” Contrast with acid’s chemical action. Avoid saying cilia kill pathogens or that all swallowed pathogens die.

visual.title: Defences at the entry points
visual.description: Four labelled examples pair a defence with a mechanism: skin barrier, mucus and cilia in airways, lysozyme in tears, hydrochloric acid in the stomach. These reduce entry or survival, not a perfect shield.

elements.text:
Airway mucus + cilia
Trap material,
then move it

Tears: lysozyme
Damages some
bacterial walls

Stomach acid
Kills many swallowed
pathogens
Barriers reduce entry or survival; they are not perfect.

slides.title: Recognise the antigen
body: An antigen can trigger a specific immune response.
Antibodies are proteins made by specialised cells.
Binding depends on the antigen.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I have a cell that makes proteins, and a protein that binds a target. They are not the same object. The simplified shape lets me predict which target fits; real binding depends on molecular structure.” Antibodies may neutralise/mark; other cells can engulf.

visual.title: A protein can recognise a specific antigen
visual.description: Simplified shape-matching model, not molecular scale: antibody protein has binding sites complementary to antigen X. Antigen Y is a different shape. Binding helps the immune response; antibodies are not cells and do not themselves engulf pathogens.

elements.text: A protein can recognise a specific antigen
A simplified recognition model; shapes are not to scale.

slides.title: Read the time and amount
body: At day 4: first response 2 units; later response 20.
The later response begins sooner in this model.
Memory lymphocytes support the faster response.
slides.notes: Model read x-axis first, then compare y-values at the same elapsed day. “20−2=18 units more, in this constructed dataset. It does not tell me an individual’s protection or a universal time.” Later exposure is to the same antigen; no universal-antibody claim.

visual.title: Same antigen: compare the responses
visual.description: Constructed teaching data comparing elapsed days after first and later exposure to the same antigen. Arbitrary antibody units: first response 0,0,2,6,10,7; later response 0,8,20,32,30,24 at days 0,2,4,6,8,10. Not clinical measurements or a protective threshold.

slides.title: Build the explanation chain
body: W1. Order: antibody response • antigen exposure • memory retained • faster later response.
Give each arrow a reason.
slides.notes: Correct exposure → specific antibody response and formation of memory → memory retained → faster response on later exposure to same antigen. Antibody production and memory formation overlap; avoid a strict claim that memory waits until every antibody disappears.
slides.reveal: Antigen exposure triggers a specific response and memory formation. Memory retained → faster response to the same antigen later.

slides.title: Choose a target, test the fit
body: W2. Would an X-specific antibody necessarily bind Y?
Explain what the model can and cannot show.
slides.notes: No: a different antigen may not have a complementary binding site. The drawing models specificity, not actual molecular scale or all immune mechanisms. Let pupils trace/point before revealing.

visual.title: A protein can recognise a specific antigen
visual.description: Simplified shape-matching model, not molecular scale: antibody protein has binding sites complementary to antigen X. Antigen Y is a different shape. Binding helps the immune response; antibodies are not cells and do not themselves engulf pathogens.

elements.text: A protein can recognise a specific antigen
A simplified recognition model; shapes are not to scale.

slides.title: Evidence desk: compare day 6
body: W3. Find each day-6 amount and the difference.
Explain one reason and one limit.
slides.notes: 6 versus 32 arbitrary units; difference 26. Memory supports faster/larger response to same antigen. Numbers constructed; graph not a clinical forecast.

table.caption: Constructed teaching data; arbitrary units, not protective thresholds.

slides.title: Which mechanism is correct?
body: Choose one explanation and defend it.
slides.notes: B correct. Use protein/cell wordcards if A; refer antigen X/Y if C; distinguish medicine mechanisms if D.

options.feedback: Antibodies are proteins; memory lymphocytes are cells.

options.text: Memory lymphocytes support a faster response to the same antigen.
options.feedback: Yes. Specific memory helps the later response begin sooner and often become larger.

options.text: One antibody protects equally against every pathogen.
options.feedback: Antibody binding is specific; different antigen features may not be recognised.

options.text: Antibiotics work by creating immune memory.
options.feedback: Antibiotics act against bacteria. They are not a method for creating specific immune memory.

slides.title: Create a defence explanation
body: Choose the agreed response page.
Use an arrow chain, short sentences or a narrated diagram.
slides.notes: Set selected route and shared evidence; pupils need no online research.

slides.title: Make the model teach someone
body: Include a barrier, recognition and memory.
Use one numerical comparison from the graph.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. Assess the cell/protein distinction before asking longer explanations. If needed, place lymphocyte and antibody in separate boxes with makes between them.

slides.title: Audience test: is the mechanism clear?
body: L1. Share one part of the explanation.
Audience: “Which is a cell? Which is a protein?”
slides.notes: Allow quiet partner/TA exchange. Pupil improves a label or arrow using the question, or defends an accurate one.

slides.title: Improve the final claim
body: “The vaccine gives perfect protection forever.”
Replace certainty with a careful mechanism.
slides.notes: Model: vaccination stimulates a specific response and memory; later exposure can be dealt with faster, reducing disease risk/severity, but protection varies and is not guaranteed. Do not introduce schedules or individual advice.

slides.title: Explain the faster response
body: E 1. Name one barrier and its action.
E 2. Is an antibody a cell or protein?
E 3. How does memory help next time?
slides.notes: Collect one accurate mechanism each. E 3 should include same antigen and faster response. Revisit matching model if universal protection appears.

slides.title: Choose the next useful step
body: Barrier action • specific binding • memory • graph reading.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute. Pupils choose privately. No health or vaccination status is requested.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Defence and memory cards
pupilPages.intro: Models and teaching summaries, not personal medical guidance.

cards.title: Barrier card
cards.text: Skin limits entry. Airway mucus traps material and cilia move it towards the throat.

cards.title: Chemical defence card
cards.text: Lysozyme in tears can damage bacterial cell walls. Stomach acid kills many swallowed pathogens.

cards.title: Recognition card
cards.text: An antigen triggers a specific response. Some lymphocytes develop into antibody-secreting cells.

cards.title: Antibody card
cards.text: Antibodies are proteins with specific binding sites. Binding helps neutralise a target or marks it for other immune action.

cards.title: Memory card
cards.text: Some lymphocytes persist as memory cells. Later exposure to the same antigen can trigger a faster, larger response.

cards.title: Vaccine card
cards.text: Vaccines expose the immune system to antigens, or instructions for making them, to develop protection and memory without needing the full disease. Protection is not a guarantee.

blocks.text: Constructed teaching data: arbitrary antibody units, not clinical results or a protection threshold.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Build the explanation
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: barrier; antigen; antibody protein; lymphocyte cell; memory; same; faster.

blocks.prompt: S1. Choose skin, mucus/cilia or stomach acid. Explain one action.
S2. Label antigen, antibody and memory lymphocyte as target feature, protein or cell.
S3. At day 4, read both amounts and calculate the difference.
S4. Complete: antigen exposure triggers a specific response and ____. A later response to the ____ antigen can be ____. Explain why.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Explain, then use evidence
pupilPages.intro: Use the defence cards and the constructed table.

blocks.prompt: M1. Explain two different barriers: one physical and one chemical.
M2. Explain the roles of antigen, antibody and memory lymphocyte without calling a protein a cell.
M3. Use day-6 data to compare first and later responses. Include the difference and a memory explanation.
M4. Explain how vaccination can prepare a later response. Why is the graph not a guarantee for one person?

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Evaluate the model
pupilPages.intro: Optional deeper reasoning. The chart compares the same antigen. Antigen Y is structurally different from X.

blocks.prompt: T1. Explain why an antibody selected for X may not bind Y. State a limit of a simple shape model.
T2. Compare the time needed to reach at least 20 units in the first and later data. What can and cannot be concluded?
T3. “Antibody levels fell, so all immune memory vanished.” Evaluate this statement.
T4. Contrast an antibiotic with a vaccine by target/mechanism. Avoid a treatment recommendation.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Keep the roles distinct
pupilPages.intro: Short sentences or labelled arrows are welcome.

blocks.prompt: E 1. One barrier and its protective action.
E 2. What kind of thing is an antibody?
E 3. Why can a response to the same antigen be faster later?
L1. What did your audience question? Record one useful revision or defended explanation.

choices: Read matched times on a graph.

answers.label: Retrieval
answers.answer: R1 disease-causing agent. R2 a barrier reduces pathogen entry. R3 cells and proteins are different; proteins are molecules made by cells.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 exposure triggers antibody response and memory formation; memory retained supports a faster later response to the same antigen. W2 no guaranteed binding to Y because its antigen structure differs; shape drawing is a simplified specificity model. W3 day 6 first 6, later 32, difference 26 arbitrary units; memory explanation, constructed-data limit.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: A false: protein versus cell. B true: specific memory supports faster secondary response. C false: recognition is specific. D false: antibiotics act against bacterial processes, not by generating specific immune memory.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: Skin physically reduces entry; mucus traps material and cilia move it towards throat; stomach hydrochloric acid kills many swallowed pathogens; lysozyme in tears can damage bacterial cell walls. M1 requires one physical and one chemical mechanism.

answers.label: S2 / M2
answers.answer: Antigen: recognised molecular feature/target that triggers response. Antibody: specific binding protein made by specialised lymphocyte-derived cells. Memory lymphocyte: long-lived cell supporting a faster later response. Core answer need not name B cells/plasma cells.

answers.label: S3
answers.answer: Day 4 first 2, later 20;20−2=18 arbitrary units more in later response.

answers.label: S4 / M4
answers.answer: Memory lymphocytes form/are retained; later exposure to the same antigen can trigger faster response. Vaccination supplies antigen or instructions for making antigen, stimulating response and memory without requiring the full disease. Graph is constructed and immunity varies; no individual guarantee.

answers.label: M3
answers.answer: Day 6 first 6, later 32; difference 26 arbitrary units. Same-antigen memory supports the faster/larger later response. This is evidence within a teaching model, not clinical proof.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: Specific binding sites need compatible antigen features. Different Y may not bind. Simple shapes omit molecular detail and the many other cell/protein interactions in immunity.

answers.label: T2
answers.answer: Later reaches 20 at day 4. First does not reach 20 in the observed 0–10 day interval. Do not say it never reaches 20 or extrapolate beyond the supplied data.

answers.label: T3
answers.answer: False inference. Antibody amount can fall while memory lymphocytes persist. Falling proteins are not evidence that every memory cell disappeared.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: Antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria and do not treat viral infection. Vaccination stimulates a specific immune response and memory; it is not an antibiotic. No clinical selection/dosing required.

answers.label: Exit and assessment
answers.answer: E 1 accurate barrier+action. E 2 protein. E 3 retained memory lymphocytes support a faster specific response on later exposure to same antigen. L1 accepts a specific correction or evidence-backed confirmation. Secure core requires roles+same antigen+faster response; reteach with cell makes protein if roles are mixed.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 10, We do 7, hinge 3, independent 11, review 3, exit 1. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing plus explanation, annotations or writing as evidence.
A quiet review still has an audience: teacher or TA reads the pupil’s decision, asks one evidence question, and the pupil revises or confirms it.

The antigen/antibody shapes and response curves are explicit conceptual models. Real immune responses involve many cell types and molecules; no universal time, dose or protective antibody threshold is claimed.

Interactive We do: predict an antigen match, test the later-response graph, explain immune memory. Paper equivalent W1–W3 uses the same diagram and data. Animation is learner-controlled and does not model a real person’s immune system.
